newsitem.title: USA: U.S. productivity jumps in first quarter.
newsitem.headline: U.S. productivity jumps in first quarter.

text.p: The productivity of U.S. businesses grew at the fastest pace in more than three years in the first quarter, allowing workers to enjoy a big rise in wages, according to government figures released on Wednesday.

The Labor Department said productivity outside the farm sector rose at an annualized pace of 2 percent in the first quarter, nearly double the 1.1 percent rate of the final three months of 1996. It was the largest rise since a 2.8 increase in the fourth quarter of 1993.
The increase in productivity fell short, however, of the 2.4 percent gain that had been expected by Wall Street economists.
With workers turning out more products for every hour worked, employers were able to pay them more without putting much upward pressure on corporate costs.

The department said that hourly compensation rose at a 4.7 percent clip in the first quarter of this year. That was larger than the 3.6 percent gain recorded in the fourth quarter last year and was the biggest increase since the first quarter of 1992, when compensation rose by 7.8 percent, a department economist said.

Unit labour costs, which reflect changes in hourly compensation and productivity, increased at a 2.7 percent annualized rate in the first quarter of this year. That was just above the 2.5 percent rate recorded in the fourth quarter and substantially over the 1 percent increase expected by economists on Wall Street.
Increases in unit labour costs often portend higher inflation down the road as companies raise prices to make up for the added costs of paying their workers.

The U.S. economy grew by 5.6 percent in the first quarter of this year, the fastest pace since the fourth quarter of 1987. Productivity often jumps when the economy surges as employers ask existing workers to put in more overtime rather than add to their staff.
